h: Glens, Lochs and Lanarkshire Days Out
p: East Kilbride has a reputation as one of Scotland's post-war new towns, all roundabouts and shopping centres, so Calderglen tends to surprise people. Drop down into the glen and you're among mature woods, waterfalls and the Rotten Calder Water cutting through the rock, with the town almost completely out of sight. It's a proper green escape on Glasgow's doorstep.

The country park has a network of paths, some easy and buggy-friendly near the visitor area, others steeper and rougher down by the river. If you've got toddlers, stick to the upper paths near the zoo; if you've got older children who like a scramble, the glen trails are the real adventure. Either way, sturdy footwear is a good idea, as it can be muddy after rain.

Make it a bigger day by heading to James Hamilton Heritage Park on the other side of East Kilbride, where a loch is used for watersports and has a path around the edge that's perfect for scooters. A little further afield, Chatelherault Country Park near Hamilton has a grand hunting lodge, gorge walks and plenty of open space. Both work nicely with the zoo for a budget-friendly weekend.

Getting there: East Kilbride has a railway station with services from Glasgow Central, and buses run across town, though a car makes it easier to reach the park itself. Bring a flask and something for lunch; a picnic in the glen beats a café queue any day.

It's a friendly, low-key spot, and that's why local families keep coming back. It works just as well on a sunny Saturday in summer as on a crisp, bright winter morning when the glen is at its quietest.
